source: Sweller, van Merrienboer, Paas (2019) Cognitive architecture and instructional design: 20 years later
finding: Worked example effect first reported by Sweller and Cooper (1985) in algebra. Studying a full solution beats solving the equivalent problem for novices. Examples focus attention on problem states and operators (solution steps), so learners can induce general solutions.
numbers: No effect size given in this review. Origin: Sweller & Cooper 1985, Cognition and Instruction 2(1):59-89.
quote: focus the learners' attention on problem states and associated operators (i.e. solution steps)
limits: Review calls the evidence very strong but gives no pooled numbers. Design of good examples is hard. Less effective for high-expertise learners.
agent_relevance: A scaffold can show full solved cases with explicit state-and-operator steps before asking the model to solve. Matches the subgoal library idea.

source: Sweller, van Merrienboer, Paas (2019) Cognitive architecture and instructional design: 20 years later
finding: Cognitive architecture behind the effect: working memory is limited only for novel information; long-term memory holds schemas (de Groot chess work) that remove that limit. Instruction should help store schemas in long-term memory.
numbers: Cites Miller 1956, Peterson & Peterson 1959, de Groot 1965, Ericsson & Kintsch 1995 (long-term working memory).
limits: Theory-level claim. Human working-memory limits do not map one to one onto an LLM context window.
agent_relevance: For an LLM the analogue of long-term memory is the library of stored solved cases and subgoal templates. Retrieve them rather than re-derive.

source: Sweller, van Merrienboer, Paas (2019) Cognitive architecture and instructional design: 20 years later
finding: Means-ends analysis (conventional problem solving) is expensive for working memory: it holds current state, goal state, differences, operators and sub-goals. It bears little relation to schema building. Goal-free problems (Sweller & Levine 1982) cut that load.
numbers: Goal-free effect is the oldest CLT effect (1982); worked example effect 1985.
quote: conventional problems ... solved by means-ends analysis, a process that is exceptionally expensive of working memory capacity
limits: Explanation is theoretical; the review says many early experiments did not measure load directly.
agent_relevance: Do not force goal-driven search on a new problem type. First study a solved case, then solve. Supports an example-first state before solving.

source: Sweller, van Merrienboer, Paas (2019) Cognitive architecture and instructional design: 20 years later
finding: Three load types and a revision. Intrinsic load = element interactivity, set by the material and the learner's knowledge. Extraneous load = set by the instructional procedure. Germane load is now treated as redistributing working memory from extraneous to intrinsic activity, not as extra load.
numbers: Seven effects in the 1998 paper; most due to extraneous load; the variability effect is the exception (intrinsic load).
limits: The three-load model is contested (see the sibling subfield on critiques). The germane load definition changed between 1998 and 2019.
agent_relevance: Use worked examples to cut extraneous load; do not claim a measured germane gain.

source: Sweller, van Merrienboer, Paas (2019) Cognitive architecture and instructional design: 20 years later
finding: Boundary: expertise reversal. As expertise rises, element interactivity falls; the worked example effect shrinks, vanishes and can reverse. Guidance should fade. Completion strategy (van Merrienboer & Krammer 1990): full examples, then completion problems with larger gaps, then full problems.
numbers: Cites Kalyuga et al. 2003, 2012. Completion problems proposed 1987 for programming.
quote: With increases in expertise, these same activities may become redundant
limits: Review level only; reversal effect sizes are in sibling documents on expertise.
agent_relevance: Adapt example density to difficulty: show full steps on new types, fade to blanks as the model succeeds. A fading rule driven by code-checked success.

source: Sweller, van Merrienboer, Paas (2019) Cognitive architecture and instructional design: 20 years later
finding: Element interactivity moderates the effect. Chen, Kalyuga, Sweller (2015, 2016, 2017): a worked example effect on high element interactivity maths (solving problems); a reverse effect (generating beats being shown) on low element interactivity material (learning definitions).
numbers: Direction only in this review.
limits: Direction only; N and effect sizes are not in this source.
agent_relevance: Examples help for multi-step procedures, not for isolated facts. Use them for procedures, not for lookup.

source: Sweller, van Merrienboer, Paas (2019) Cognitive architecture and instructional design: 20 years later
finding: Split-attention: a worked example with a diagram and separate text forces mental integration; physically integrating them restores the example effect (Tarmizi & Sweller 1988; Chandler & Sweller 1992). Self-explanation prompts on examples can help if total load stays within capacity (Renkl et al. 1998).
numbers: No numbers in this source.
limits: Self-explanation help is conditional on load; Barbieri 2023 meta-analysis finds prompts do not add (see a08).
agent_relevance: Put the step, its reason and its check in the same text block of an example.

source: Barbieri, Miller-Cotto, Booth (2023) A meta-analysis of the worked examples effect on mathematics performance
finding: Main effect: worked examples help maths performance, from elementary school to postsecondary.
numbers: 8033 abstracts screened; 43 articles, 55 studies, 181 effect sizes; robust variance estimation; average g = 0.48 (p = 0.01), medium.
limits: Only the abstract page was readable (paywall), not the full paper. Includes correct, incorrect and mixed examples.
agent_relevance: Best single pooled estimate for how much example study should help in maths: about half a standard deviation.

source: Barbieri et al. (2023) meta-analysis (abstract page)
finding: Moderators: correct examples alone gave larger effects than incorrect examples alone or correct plus incorrect combined. Self-explanation prompts moderated the effect NEGATIVELY compared with examples without prompts. The effect was medium whether used for practice or initial skill acquisition.
numbers: Moderators tested: example type, self-explanation prompts, timing (practice vs skill acquisition). Per-moderator g is not in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Contradicts the common claim that self-explanation prompts add value. The incorrect-example advantage is not supported here.
agent_relevance: Be careful with designs that contrast wrong examples. Correct examples first. Do not assume that prompting the model to explain each step adds gains.

source: Nathan, Mertz, Ryan (1994) Learning through self-explanation of mathematics examples: effects of cognitive load (AERA paper, ERIC ED372095)
finding: Conceptual extension of the worked example idea with self-explanation (SE) in algebra. Story-problem translation: studying examples beat generating solutions; SE beat no-SE; SE x load interaction.
numbers: n = 32 (Pittsburgh subject pool), 2 x 2 (SE x load), 1-2 week delay. Translation: SE main effect F(1,25)=5.9, p<.025; load main effect F(1,25)=6.76, p<.02; interaction F(1,25)=7.1, p<.02. Manipulation: no significant effects; interaction t(25)=1.7, p=.1.
limits: Small N; conference paper; the procedural manipulation task showed only a weak pattern, authors blame the delay. Examples were removed after study, as in Sweller & Cooper 1985.
agent_relevance: Self-explanation helped most on conceptual translation tasks, little on procedural manipulation. Explaining while also generating a solution gave no gain: load competition.

source: Nathan et al. (1994) AERA paper
finding: Non-explainers show the Sweller & Cooper 1985 pattern: solution generation (high load) impairs later performance; but the gap was not significant after the delay.
numbers: High vs low load difference for non-self-explainers not significant (overlapping error bars); SE improvement about 20% higher on translation on average.
limits: The authors' explanation (the 1-2 week delay) is a guess. Boundary condition: the example advantage can wash out at delay.
agent_relevance: Test the benefit after a delay or on fresh problems, not only on the immediately following one.

source: Nathan et al. (1994) AERA paper
finding: Competing accounts of why examples work: (1) learning happens at study time (self-explanation fills gaps; VanLehn & Jones 1993) versus (2) learning happens later during knowledge compilation when the example is used in a new problem (Trafton & Reiser 1993: separating target from source hurt transfer).
numbers: Cited accounts; no new numbers.
limits: Authors say their data may challenge the knowledge compilation view.
agent_relevance: Two mechanisms to keep: store the example, and use it by analogy later. A scaffold needs both retrieval of cases and an explicit mapping step.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Worked-example effect (secondary summary of the literature)
finding: Secondary summary lists boundary conditions and replications: Kalyuga et al. 2000, 2001 expertise reversal in three studies (mechanical engineering diagrams, relay circuits, programming logic); Nievelstein et al. 2013: effect held for both novice and advanced law students on a less structured task; Quilici & Mayer: three examples per type versus one gave no difference in sorting new problems; Paas: completion problems as good as fully worked ones.
numbers: No sample sizes on the page. van Gog, Kester, Paas 2011: electrical circuit troubleshooting; worked-example-only and example-problem pairs beat problem-example pairs and problem solving, with lower mental effort.
limits: Wikipedia; each claim needs checking against the original paper. Used only to list leads.
agent_relevance: Leads for the boundary list: ill-structured domains may keep the effect; more examples do not always mean more transfer.

source: Lechner, Moser, Pander, Geist, Lewalter (2024) Learning scientific observation with worked examples in a digital learning environment
finding: Recent field experiment, 62 university students. Worked-example videos helped application of knowledge; FADED examples gave no extra advantage over non-faded examples. Extraneous load and motivation differences were in the expected direction but not significant.
numbers: N = 62, three groups (faded WE, non-faded WE, control). Overall MANOVA F(12,106)=2.59, p=.005, eta2=.23. Application of knowledge F(2,57)=13.26, p<.001, eta2=.32. Extraneous CL F(2,57)=2.68, p=.065, eta2=.09. Factual knowledge change F(2,57)=2.93, p=.062.
limits: Quasi-experimental; high pretest scores (ceiling); heuristic examples in biology, not maths.
agent_relevance: A case where the fading advantage (Renkl 2002) did not appear. Fading may add little when learners already know much.

source: He-Yueya, Goodman, Brunskill (2024) Evaluating and Optimizing Educational Content with Large Language Model Judgments
finding: GPT-3.5 used as a simulated educational expert replicates two CLT findings in text: expertise reversal (worked examples help low-expertise personas, no difference for high-expertise) and the variability effect (high variability helps only in worked-example conditions). The paper also describes the original human studies it imitates.
numbers: 120 simulated student personas, skill levels 1-5; 8 problems (worked solutions for odd items); gpt-3.5-turbo-16k, temperature 0. Human original: 42 Year 9 students, coordinate geometry (Kalyuga et al. 2001 Exp 3); variability: 60 fourth-year secondary students (Paas & van Merrienboer 1994).
limits: LM judges may have seen the literature in training; the paper says so. Scores are LM judgments, not real learning. Exact scores shown only in figures.
agent_relevance: Shows an LLM knows the example effect and its limits. A scaffold could use a model judge to choose how much to show, but G5 says a judge must be blind to authorship; treat it as a hint only.

source: He-Yueya et al. (2024)
finding: Instruction optimization loop: one LM writes worksheets, another LM predicts post-test scores for a persona. The authors report gains for math word-problem worksheets under the LM reward.
numbers: K candidates per step, memory of best instruction-score pairs; results in figures only.
limits: Reward is a simulated judgment, so gains may not carry to real learners.
agent_relevance: Pattern for tuning example sets: generate, score by an outcome, keep the best. For our agent the score must be a real check, not an LM guess.

source: Simonds, Lau, Bandi (2024) REL: Working out is all you need
finding: Fine-tuning on worked solutions that show the process (brainstorming, testing hypotheses, backtracking) beat fine-tuning on standard AIME step solutions. 100 human-made worked solutions gave 18.89% on AIME 2024 for GPT-4o-mini (base 6.66%); AIME solutions stayed at 4-6% from 1 to 1,000 samples.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini base 6.66%; Human FT 18.89% at 100 examples (+12.2 points); AIME FT flat 4-6%; 10 to 100 examples gave +7.8 points; REL pipeline on GPT-4o reached 27.78% vs 12% base. Authors say 100 worked solutions beat 1000 standard ones (5.56%).
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed. AIME 2024 has 30 problems, so one problem is 3.3 points; single run. This is training, not prompting; the paper says prompting alone did not elicit the behaviour.
agent_relevance: Process-rich examples (what a human does, including errors and fixes) taught more than clean solutions. For a subgoal library: store the search and the repair, not only the neat final steps.

source: Simonds et al. (2024) REL
finding: REL loop: generator makes a worked solution, a GPT-4o verifier with the reference solution gives a hint when it is wrong, the generator rewrites acknowledging the error; after two failed hint rounds the full solution is given and folded in.
numbers: Two hint rounds, then full solution; 100 samples per iteration; smaller models were trained on GPT-4o output because their own worked solutions were poor.
limits: Verifier sees the reference answer, so this is not a self-check. Small models made poor worked solutions.
agent_relevance: Mirrors fading and repair. Warns that the model writing the examples must be strong enough.

source: Wei et al. (2022) Chain-of-thought prompting elicits reasoning in large language models
finding: Few-shot exemplars that include step-by-step reasoning are worked examples for a model. PaLM 540B with eight such exemplars reached state of the art on GSM8K, above fine-tuned GPT-3 with a verifier.
numbers: GSM8K PaLM 540B: standard prompting 17.9%, chain of thought 56.9% (+39.0). Gains largest on harder sets; SingleOp, the easiest set, showed negative or very small gains. Eight hand-written exemplars; three sets drawn at random from the training set worked comparably.
limits: Emerges only in large models. Faithfulness of the chain to the model's real process is not shown.
agent_relevance: The direct LLM analogue of the worked example effect: showing steps beats showing answers, more so for multi-step problems. A sibling subfield covers CoT in depth.

source: Min et al. (2022) Rethinking the role of demonstrations: what makes in-context learning work?
finding: Boundary for example-based prompting: replacing gold labels in demonstrations with random labels barely hurts. What matters is the label space, the input distribution and the format.
numbers: Random labels: drop of 0-5% absolute across 12 models including GPT-3; multi-choice 1.7% average, classification 2.6%.
limits: Classification and multi-choice tasks, not multi-step maths. Does not say the content of reasoning steps is unimportant.
agent_relevance: Part of what examples do for a model is set format and distribution, not teach correctness. Do not credit all gains to solution content.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Towards understanding chain-of-thought prompting: an empirical study of what matters
finding: Invalid reasoning in demonstrations keeps most of the benefit; relevance to the query and correct step order matter more than validity.
numbers: text-davinci-002 on GSM8K answer accuracy: standard 15.4; chain of thought 48.5; invalid reasoning 39.5 (about 81% of CoT); no coherence 23.1; no relevance 11.0. Intrinsic recall under invalid reasoning kept over 90% of CoT in all models tested.
limits: Hand-written invalid rationales; one main model in the table; Bamboogle also reported.
agent_relevance: Parallel to Barbieri: correct examples are still best, but structure and relevance drive much of the effect. Library entries must be relevant to the query and in order.

source: Pardos & Bhandari (2023) Learning gain differences between ChatGPT and human tutor generated algebra hints (arXiv v1)
finding: Randomised test of ChatGPT worked-solution hints against human-authored hints in algebra. 70% of ChatGPT hints passed manual quality checks. In v1 only the human-hint groups showed a significant pre-to-post gain.
numbers: N = 77 MTurk (3 excluded), 2 x 2 lessons. Elementary: human hints n=19 gain 24.63% (pre 59.68, post 84.32); ChatGPT n=21 gain 11.14% (pre 74.67, post 85.81). Intermediate: human n=17 gain 23.65% (pre 50.94, post 74.59); ChatGPT n=20 gain 1.7% (pre 80.05, post 81.75). Pre-post p=.0219 and .0213 for human hints; p=.1427 and .7912 for ChatGPT hints.
limits: Pretest mismatch in Intermediate (ceiling for ChatGPT group). A later published version is reported in a search snippet as finding gains equivalent (not opened). Rows were paired by checking pre/post arithmetic.
agent_relevance: LLM-written worked solutions can fall short of human ones on first test, so generated examples need quality control by code before entering a library.

source: Sweller (2010) Element interactivity and intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load
finding: Element interactivity defines intrinsic load and also extraneous load; germane load is defined in terms of intrinsic load. This is the unifying account of why examples (which cut interactivity caused by search) work.
numbers: Abstract page: 1773 citations at time of access. No experimental numbers.
limits: Abstract page only. Theoretical paper.
agent_relevance: Cite when deciding what makes a step costly: the number of interacting elements the model must hold, not the step count.

source: Renkl (2017) Learning from worked-examples in mathematics: students relate procedures to principles
finding: Renkl argues worked examples help because learners interrelate principles with several problem cases, giving an interconnected structure that supports transfer. He answers objections from maths education such as the neglect of typical student errors.
numbers: Abstract only: no numbers.
quote: students profit more from studying worked examples as compared to solving problems
limits: Abstract page only (paywall). Rests on his own group's studies.
agent_relevance: Library entries should name the principle behind each step and be linked across cases, not be isolated recipes.

source: Sweller & Cooper (1985) The use of worked examples as a substitute for problem solving in learning algebra
finding: Founding paper. Five experiments in algebra; hypothesis that conventional search retards schema acquisition. Learners studying worked-out example-problem pairs did better on later problems than learners who solved the same problems.
numbers: A secondary note says in Experiment 5 study groups took about half the time and made one fifth of the errors on similar problems; unverified.
limits: Not opened (paper not accessible). The effect did not seem to extend to problems varied on the posttest (secondary summary).
agent_relevance: Founding evidence is similar-problem transfer only; do not assume transfer to new problem types.

source: Cooper & Sweller (1987) Effects of schema acquisition and rule automation on mathematical problem-solving transfer
finding: Follow-up cited by the reviews: examples help via schema acquisition and rule automation; far transfer needs schema acquisition.
numbers: Not opened; no numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. Details come only from citations.
agent_relevance: Relevant to what a library should store: schemas versus automated rules.

source: Ward & Sweller (1990) Structuring effective worked examples
finding: Boundary: under some conditions worked examples are no more effective, and possibly less effective, than solving problems; examples must be structured to avoid split attention.
numbers: Not opened. Quote taken from the Wikipedia article's citation of the paper.
limits: Not opened; second hand.
agent_relevance: Badly formatted examples (split across sources) remove the benefit; format an example as one block.

source: Chi, Bassok, Lewis, Reimann, Glaser (1989) Self-explanations: how students study and use examples in learning to solve problems
finding: Better physics problem solvers explained examples more actively to themselves (inferences, links to prior knowledge, monitoring). Cited as the origin of self-explanation work by Nathan 1994 and Sweller 2019.
numbers: Not opened; numbers not recorded.
limits: Not opened. Observational (good vs poor solvers), not causal; Nathan reports a later prompted-biology study as the causal step.
agent_relevance: Self-explanation is one route; Barbieri 2023 suggests prompting may not add to examples in maths.

source: Renkl, Atkinson, Maier, Staley (2002); Atkinson, Renkl, Merrill (2003) fading of worked examples
finding: Fading steps out of worked examples improved near transfer over example-problem pairs; the effect was not reliable on far transfer (from search snippets). Lechner 2024 found no extra fading benefit.
numbers: Not opened; snippet only, no numbers.
limits: Not opened; snippets only. Far transfer effect unreliable.
agent_relevance: Fading helps repeated problem types; do not expect it to fix new problem types.

source: Kalyuga, Chandler, Tuovinen, Sweller (2001) When problem solving is superior to studying worked examples
finding: Core boundary evidence for expertise reversal: as learners gain knowledge, studying examples becomes worse than solving problems. Cited by Sweller 2019 and He-Yueya 2024.
numbers: Not opened; He-Yueya describes Exp 3 as 42 Year 9 students, coordinate geometry.
limits: Not opened; second hand via He-Yueya 2024.
agent_relevance: Condition the number of shown steps on success on the type so far.
